questions.q: State what is meant by multitasking.

markPoints.concept: the operating system appears to run several programs at the same time
markPoints.exemplar: Running several programs at what appears to be the same time.

questions.example: The operating system running several programs at what appears to the user to be the same time, by switching between them very quickly.
questions.paraphrase: Several applications appearing to run together, because the system swaps between them rapidly.
questions.feedback: More than one program at once. On a single core it only appears simultaneous, which is worth saying.

questions.q: Explain how an operating system makes several programs appear to run at the same time on a single-core processor.

markPoints.concept: only one program can actually use the processor at any instant
accept: one|only one|a single|at a time|at once
markPoints.exemplar: Only one program can use the processor at any one moment.

markPoints.concept: so the operating system gives each program a short turn in rotation
markPoints.exemplar: The operating system gives each program a short turn in rotation.

markPoints.concept: and the switching is so fast that the user does not notice
accept: so fast|very fast|quickly|rapid|milliseconds|does not notice|cannot tell|appears|seems|looks like
markPoints.exemplar: The switching is so fast that it appears simultaneous to the user.

questions.example: A single core can only execute one program's instructions at any instant, so the operating system gives each program a very short slice of processor time in turn and then switches to the next one. The switching happens thousands of times a second, so to the user everything appears to be running at once.
questions.paraphrase: Because the processor can only handle one program at a time, the system allocates each a brief slot before moving to the next, and it does this so rapidly that the user cannot tell they are taking turns.
questions.feedback: Three ideas: one at a time, turns, and why it looks simultaneous.

questions.q: State one thing the operating system does when it manages memory.

markPoints.concept: it decides where each program's data goes and stops programs overwriting each other
markPoints.exemplar: It allocates each program its own space in memory.

questions.example: It allocates each program its own area of memory and stops one program from overwriting another's data.
questions.paraphrase: It assigns space to each program and keeps them from interfering with one another.
questions.feedback: Allocating, and keeping programs apart. Either half earns the mark.

questions.q: State what a device driver does.

markPoints.concept: it lets the operating system communicate with a particular piece of hardware
markPoints.exemplar: It lets the operating system communicate with a piece of hardware.

questions.example: It translates between the operating system and a particular piece of hardware, so the operating system can use the device without knowing how it works inside.
questions.paraphrase: It allows the system software to control a specific device.
questions.feedback: Between the operating system and the device. A driver is a translator, not a program the user runs.

questions.q: A user plugs in a new printer and it does not work until software is installed. What has been installed?
questions.feedback: Every model of hardware needs its own driver, which is why a new device often needs one installed.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 2 — Multitasking floor, station 4: Virtual memory

questions.q: Put these steps in the order the operating system carries them out when it switches between two programs.
steps: The first program's turn runs out
The operating system saves where that program had got to
The operating system loads where the second program had got to
The second program runs for its turn
The operating system saves the second program's position in its turn
questions.feedback: Saving where a program had got to is the whole trick: without it the program could not carry on from the same place.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 2 — Multitasking floor, station 2: Sharing the processor

questions.q: A computer with one processor core appears to run six programs at once. What is actually happening?
options: The processor is switching between them very quickly
All six are running in the same instant
Five of them are paused until the first finishes
The programs are sharing one set of instructions
questions.feedback: One core, one instruction at a time. The speed of the switching is what makes it look simultaneous.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 2 — Multitasking floor, station 2: Sharing the processor

markPoints.concept: space on secondary storage used as if it were RAM when RAM is full
accept: as if it were ram|as though it were ram|as though it is ram|like ram|instead of ram|extra ram|pretend|acts as ram|used as ram|ram is full|ram runs out|stand in for ram|stands in for ram|stand in for main memory|stands in for main memory
markPoints.exemplar: Space on the hard disk used as though it were RAM when RAM is full.

questions.example: An area of secondary storage that the operating system uses as though it were RAM, when the programs running need more memory than the RAM can hold.
questions.paraphrase: Part of the hard drive set aside to stand in for main memory once that memory is full.
questions.feedback: Disk standing in for RAM. Saying it is more RAM is not quite the answer.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 2 — Multitasking floor, station 4: Virtual memory

questions.q: Explain why a computer using virtual memory heavily feels slow.

markPoints.concept: secondary storage is far slower to read and write than RAM
accept: slower|slow|not as fast|less quick|longer|thousands of times|takes more time
markPoints.exemplar: Secondary storage is far slower to read and write than RAM.

markPoints.concept: and the operating system keeps moving pages between the two
markPoints.exemplar: This means the operating system spends its time moving data back and forth instead of running programs.

questions.example: Reading and writing secondary storage takes thousands of times longer than reading RAM, and when memory is short the operating system is constantly moving data out to the disk and back again. The processor ends up waiting for the disk rather than running the programs.
questions.paraphrase: Because the drive is so much slower than main memory, and data has to be shifted between the two over and over, the machine spends its time transferring rather than computing.
questions.feedback: Slower storage, and the constant moving. Both halves.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 2 — Multitasking floor, station 4: Virtual memory

questions.q: A user plugs in a USB memory stick and it works immediately with no software to install. What makes this possible?
options: The operating system already has a driver for that kind of device
The memory stick contains its own operating system
The memory stick does not need a driver
The user must have installed one earlier that day
questions.feedback: Common kinds of device have drivers built into the operating system, which is what plug and play means.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 2 — Multitasking floor, station 6: Updates and plug and play

questions.q: Explain why an operating system needs updating.

markPoints.concept: newly found security weaknesses have to be closed
markPoints.exemplar: Updates close security weaknesses that have been found since it was released.

markPoints.concept: and new hardware and software need support that did not exist before
markPoints.exemplar: They also add support for new hardware and fix faults that have been found.

questions.example: Weaknesses are found in any operating system after it is released, and an update closes them before an attacker can use them. Updates also add support for hardware and software that did not exist when the system shipped, and fix faults that have come to light.
questions.paraphrase: Flaws that attackers could exploit are patched, and support is added for devices and programs that were not around when the system was written.
questions.feedback: Security, and keeping up with new things. Either pair earns both marks.
